policies.state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
policies.summary: Since 2026-07-15 an applicant for a wind facility certificate must certify that turbines will not be artificially lit except as required by law and that shadow flicker will be minimized and will not significantly harm neighboring uses, and the board considers compliance when deciding.

policies.state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
policies.summary: A merchant generating facility of 10 MW or more that sells at wholesale needs a construction certificate from the state siting board, and local ordinances, permits and planning and zoning setbacks still apply and prevail over a conflicting board order. Smaller facilities are left to local government.

policies.state_body: Kentucky State Board on Electric Generation and Transmission Siting
policies.summary: A siting board certificate may not issue unless any wind turbine is at least 1,000 feet from adjoining property lines and all generating structures are 2,000 feet from any residential neighborhood, school, hospital or nursing home; since 2026-07-15 wind turbine hub height is capped at 350 feet. Local planning and zoning limits take precedence where adopted, and the board may grant deviations from the state distances.

Breckinridge County, Kentucky Ordinance 2025-0121 (Solar Energy Systems), second reading Feb. 17, 2025 (4-3), repealed and replaced Ordinance 2022-0321. Large-scale solar must be set back 1,000 ft from non-participating property lines and from public road and rail rights-of-way, and 2,000 ft from churches, schools, hospitals, residential buildings and incorporated city limits; the fiscal court may set more or less stringent setbacks case by case. In Clover Creek Solar Project LLC v. Breckinridge County Fiscal Court, the Kentucky Court of Appeals reversed the circuit court and held the ordinance invalid because the county has no planning and zoning commission under KRS Chapter 100; the county's motion for discretionary review is pending at the Kentucky Supreme Court.
Prohibits ground-mounted solar panel systems from being the primary use of a property in an agricultural district if the property is smaller than ten acres.

Hopkinsville’s solar ordinance requires that certain large-scale solar projects be set back at least 1,000 feet from any lot line and at least 2,000 feet from the nearest lot line of any property containing a residential use or quasi-public use.

On April 29, 2024, the Lyon County Fiscal Court unanimously adopted Ordinance 04-2024 establishing licensing requirements for large scale solar energy systems, including rooftop solar and ground-mounted solar.

Mason County’s solar ordinance mandates that utility-scale solar projects be set back at least 500 feet from private property lines, and at least 600 or 750 feet from dwellings, schools, and many other occupied buildings, depending on the size of the property.
No more than 2,000 acres in the unincorporated areas of the county may be used for large-scale solar projects.

Villa Hills has banned commercial solar projects by requiring in its solar ordinance that the primary purpose of solar energy systems be for providing power for the property where the system is located, rather than for commercial use.
